Moreover
mōr-ō'ver
adv. (of addition; rendering Hebrew gam and the waw-consecutive, Greek de and eti)
A compound of more and over — over and above what has been said. It adds a further item to a discourse already in progress, and in the prophets it commonly opens a fresh word from the LORD in an unbroken series.

Biblical Definition

Moreover adds. It is the hinge on which a speech or a narrative turns to its next item without changing subject, and its steady recurrence in the prophets is itself instructive: God's word comes not as a single utterance but as a sustained address. “Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears” (Ezekiel 3:10) — the prophet is commissioned in stages, and this stage concerns not what he will say but how he must first receive. Zechariah's interpreting angel uses it to press an explanation further: “He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth” (Zechariah 5:6). Chronicles uses it to continue the record of a reign: “Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah” (2 Chronicles 27:4). And in ordinary conversation it does exactly what it does today, adding a detail to hospitality already offered: “She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in” (Genesis 24:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

An adverb of addition: beyond what has been said, further, besides. In Scripture it commonly introduces the next stage of a continuing discourse, and in the prophets a further word from the LORD in an unbroken series.

expand to see more

MOREOVER, adv. [more and over.] Beyond what has been said; further; besides; also.

2. It connects a new particular to a discourse already begun, without changing the subject.

3. It answers to the Hebrew gam and to the Greek de and eti.

4. Furthermore and besides are of the same class of connectives.

5. In Scripture, Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, Ezek. 3; She said moreover unto him, Gen. 24.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 3:10 — "Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears."

Zechariah 5:6 — "And I said, What is it? And he said, This is an ephah that goeth forth. He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth."

2 Chronicles 27:4 — "Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers."

Genesis 24:25 — "She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in."

Modern Corruption

Ezekiel's commission puts receiving before speaking — the word taken into the heart and heard with the ears before it is delivered. The order is regularly reversed by men who study Scripture only for what they will say of it to others.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that the messenger must first be a hearer. Ezekiel is told to receive all God's words in his heart and hear them with his ears, and only then to go to the captives and speak. The same order governs Ezra, who prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and afterward to teach in Israel statutes and judgments — seek, do, teach, in that sequence. A preacher who reverses it becomes an intermediary handling material he has never let touch him.

The danger is not confined to the pulpit. Any Christian who reads chiefly to have something to contribute — in a class, in an argument, on a screen — is exposed to it. The remedy is a habit of reading in which nothing is passed on for a time, and the first question asked of every text is what it requires of the reader himself. Ezekiel's ministry was largely unsuccessful by any visible measure, and the LORD told him beforehand that it would be; what was required of him was faithfulness in receiving and delivering, and that is what was commended.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew adds with gam (also, moreover) and with the ordinary narrative waw; Greek uses de (and, but, moreover) and eti (yet, still, further). The English compound simply joins more to over.

expand to see more

Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover, yea; the commonest additive particle.

Hebrew waw-consecutive — the narrative connective that carries a story or a discourse forward step by step.

Greek de (G1161) — and, but, moreover; a light connective marking the next item.

Greek eti (G2089) — yet, still, further; adds something beyond what was said.

Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, hearken, obey; what Ezekiel was to do before speaking.

Usage

"Of a prophet commissioned first to receive: Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words... receive in thine heart (Ezekiel 3:10)."

"Of an explanation pressed further: He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth (Zechariah 5:6)."

"Of hospitality offered with an added detail: She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough (Genesis 24:25)."
